findings.text: H5771 (avon) shows the identical bear-iniquity idiom in Lev 5:1, 5:17, 17:16, 20:17 and 20:19: the bearing-language already analysed under H5375J (nasa) in the guilt subgroup, here paired with avon instead of nasa's own object.

H5771 (avon) carries the same forgiveness-formula language as the other families: forgiving iniquity and transgression (Num 14:18, Exod 34:7), pardoning iniquity (Mic 7:18), and blotting out transgressions like mist (already cross-referenced in family G).

Isaiah 53:5, pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, cites avon (H5771G) at the same verse already found under H0817 (guilt), H5375J (bearing) and H6588 (transgression). This is now the fourth family independently converging on Isaiah 53 as a shared reference point across the M10 cluster's vocabulary.

One root (avon) independently reproduces the exact structural pattern of two other surveyed families (pesha and the guilt subgroup) at the same shared verse. Avon, pesha and the guilt subgroup's asham and nasa complex may not be four distillable families but four English-gloss windows onto one Hebrew moral-failure vocabulary cluster that treats recognition, accrual and remedy as one integrated idea, with Isaiah 53 recurring as the convergence point across all of them.

nodes.disposition_note: the line names Isaiah 53 as a whole chapter; the document's own shared verse is 53:5 (line 43)

findings.text: H1215 (betsa, 17 verses) is a narrower, specifically economic form of injustice, unjust gain: bribery, dishonest profit, corrupt religious leadership (everyone is greedy for unjust gain; from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely, Jer 6:13, 8:10) and oppressive commerce (Ezek 22:27, wolves tearing the prey to get dishonest gain). It does not overlap with avon's pattern and is the one part of this family that reads as its own concept.

Avel and avlah (H5766A/B): in Ezekiel's repeated formula, when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice he shall die (Ezek 3:20, 18:24, 18:26, 33:13, 33:18). Injustice is a moral reversal from a prior righteous state, relapse and not a starting condition, unlike guilt's recognition-model or cruelty's other-attribution, which describe a condition someone simply has or falls into.
God's own repeated self-description as one who does no injustice (Zeph 3:5, Deut 32:4, Ps 92:15) is the fixed standard the reversal of the righteous person (Ezekiel's formula) is measured against.
